title: Λαιστρυγόνες καὶ Αἰαίη
titleEn: The Laestrygonians and Circe’s Island — Odyssey 10.76–173
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, still telling his tale at the Phaeacian court, is sent off from the island of Aeolus and sails six days to Telepylus, the city of the Laestrygonians, where night and day lie so close together that a man who never slept could earn two wages. He alone moors his ship outside the narrow harbour. Three men he sends inland meet the daughter of King Antiphates, and her mother, as big as a mountain peak; Antiphates seizes one of them for his meal, and the Laestrygonians, crowding down like Giants, pelt the ships with great stones and spear the crews like fish. Odysseus cuts his cable and escapes in his one ship, glad to be out of death but grieving for his lost companions. They come to Aeaea, the island of Circe, daughter of the Sun, and lie two days worn out; on the third Odysseus climbs a lookout and sees smoke rising from her halls. On the way back to the ship a god takes pity on him and sends a great stag across his path. He kills it with his spear, binds its feet, and carries it to the ship to rouse his men.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἀπέπεμπε δόμων βαρέα στενάχοντα.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn apepempe domōn barea stenachonta.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he sent off from the house me, heavily groaning.
sentences.i: With these words he sent me off from his house as I groaned heavily.
sentences.n: These words follow Aeolus’s speech, which closed at the end of 75; the ‘he’ of ἀπέπεμπε is Aeolus, and ‘me’, the man sent away, is not written but has to be supplied for the accusative participle στενάχοντα ‘groaning’. ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’, and ἀπέπεμπε is the imperfect of ἀποπέμπω, the same ‘send off’ that Aeolus used at 73 of what he would not do. βαρέα, a neuter plural used as an adverb, is ‘heavily’. δόμων is a plural standing for his one house. A new paragraph begins.

sentences.t: ἔνθεν δὲ προτέρω πλέομεν ἀκαχήμενοι ἦτορ.
sentences.tr: enthen de proterō pleomen akachēmenoi ētor.
sentences.l: From there farther we sailed, grieved in heart;
sentences.i: From there we sailed on, grieved at heart.
sentences.n: This is the formula of 9.62, which returns in full at 133; here it stands alone and ends at ἦτορ. ἔνθεν is ‘from there’ and προτέρω ‘farther on’; πλέομεν is an unaugmented imperfect, the same form as the present. ἀκαχήμενοι, from ἀκαχίζω, is a perfect participle ‘grieved’, with ἦτορ an accusative of respect: ‘grieved in heart’. At 9.62 the grief is for dead companions; here no one has yet been lost, and the next lines give the reason.

sentences.t:
τείρετο δ’ ἀνδρῶν θυμὸς ὑπ’ εἰρεσίης ἀλεγεινῆς
ἡμετέρῃ ματίῃ, ἐπεὶ οὐκέτι φαίνετο πομπή.
sentences.tr:
teireto d’ andrōn thymos hyp’ eiresiēs alegeinēs
hēmeterēi matiēi, epei ouketi phaineto pompē.
sentences.l:
And was worn down of the men the heart under the grievous rowing,
by our foolishness, since no longer did an escort appear.
sentences.i: And the men’s hearts were worn down by the grievous rowing, through our foolishness, since no escort appeared any longer.
sentences.n: This gives the reason for the men’s low spirits. θυμὸς ἀνδρῶν is ‘the heart of the men’, one heart for the whole crew, and τείρετο is the imperfect passive of τείρω ‘wear down’. ὑπ’ with the genitive εἰρεσίης ἀλεγεινῆς gives the cause, ‘by the grievous rowing’. ἡμετέρῃ ματίῃ is a dative of cause, ‘by our foolishness’: ματίη is ‘folly, a fruitless act’, and the folly is the opening of the skin (10.44–47), which 10.27 called ἀφραδίῃσιν ‘follies’. πομπή is ‘escort’: the escort home was the West Wind that Aeolus had sent (10.25), and the clause says only that it no longer shows itself.

sentences.t:
ἑξῆμαρ μὲν ὁμῶς πλέομεν νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ,
ἑβδομάτῃ δ’ ἱκόμεσθα Λάμου αἰπὺ πτολίεθρον,
Τηλέπυλον Λαιστρυγονίην, ὅθι ποιμένα ποιμὴν
ἠπύει εἰσελάων, ὁ δέ τ’ ἐξελάων ὑπακούει.
sentences.tr:
hexēmar men homōs pleomen nyktas te kai ēmar,
hebdomatēi d’ hikomestha Lamou aipy ptoliethron,
Tēlepylon Laistrygoniēn, hothi poimena poimēn
ēpyei eiselaōn, ho de t’ exelaōn hypakouei.
sentences.l:
Six days alike we sailed, both nights and day,
and on the seventh we came to Lamus’ steep citadel,
Laestrygonian Telepylus, where shepherd to shepherd
calls out, driving in, and the other, driving out, answers.
sentences.i: For six days and nights together we sailed on, and on the seventh we came to Lamus’ steep citadel, Laestrygonian Telepylus, where one shepherd calls to another as he drives in, and the other, as he drives out, answers.
sentences.n: This is 10.28 with ἑξῆμαρ ‘for six days’ for ἐννῆμαρ ‘for nine days’. ἑβδομάτῃ is a dative of time, ‘on the seventh’, and ἱκόμεσθα is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι with the ending -μεσθα for -μεθα: ‘we came to’. Λάμου αἰπὺ πτολίεθρον is ‘the steep citadel of Lamus’ (αἰπύς ‘steep’; πτολίεθρον ‘citadel’, as at 1.2), and Τηλέπυλον Λαιστρυγονίην, ‘Laestrygonian Telepylus’, names it. In the relative clause ποιμένα ποιμήν is ‘shepherd (acc.) … shepherd (nom.)’; ἠπύει is ‘calls out to’; εἰσελάων and ἐξελάων are uncontracted participles ‘driving in’ and ‘driving out’ (Attic εἰσελαύνων, ἐξελαύνων), with the flocks left unsaid; and ὁ δέ τ’ is ‘and the other’, with epic τε.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα κ’ ἄυπνος ἀνὴρ δοιοὺς ἐξήρατο μισθούς,
τὸν μὲν βουκολέων, τὸν δ’ ἄργυφα μῆλα νομεύων·
sentences.tr:
entha k’ aypnos anēr doious exērato misthous,
ton men boukoleōn, ton d’ argypha mēla nomeuōn·
sentences.l:
There a sleepless man two wages might have earned,
the one by herding cattle, the other by pasturing silver-white flocks;
sentences.i: A sleepless man could have earned two wages there, one by herding cattle and the other by pasturing the silver-white flocks;
sentences.n: ἄυπνος ἀνήρ, ‘a sleepless man’, is a supposed man, not one the travellers meet: the line says what such a man could do here. κε with the aorist ἐξήρατο (ἐξαίρομαι ‘take out for oneself, win’) is a past possibility, ‘could have earned’, and δοιοὺς μισθούς is ‘two wages’. τὸν μὲν … τὸν δ’ are ‘the one … the other’, one for each wage, with βουκολέων ‘herding cattle’ and νομεύων ‘pasturing’. ἄργυφα, ‘silver-white’, describes the flocks, and μῆλα is the house ‘flocks’.

sentences.t: ἐγγὺς γὰρ νυκτός τε καὶ ἤματός εἰσι κέλευθοι.
sentences.tr: engys gar nyktos te kai ēmatos eisi keleuthoi.
sentences.l: for near are of night and of day the paths.
sentences.i: for the paths of night and of day lie close together.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason a sleepless man could draw two wages: the paths of night and of day lie close together. The poem does not say why they do. κέλευθοι is ‘paths, ways’, as in ὑγρὰ κέλευθα ‘the watery ways’, and νυκτός τε καὶ ἤματος are genitives depending on it; ἐγγύς is ‘near’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἐπεὶ ἐς λιμένα κλυτὸν ἤλθομεν, ὃν πέρι πέτρη
ἠλίβατος τετύχηκε διαμπερὲς ἀμφοτέρωθεν,
ἀκταὶ δὲ προβλῆτες ἐναντίαι ἀλλήλῃσιν
ἐν στόματι προύχουσιν, ἀραιὴ δ’ εἴσοδός ἐστιν,
sentences.tr:
enth’ epei es limena klyton ēlthomen, hon peri petrē
ēlibatos tetychēke diamperes amphoterōthen,
aktai de problētes enantiai allēlēisin
en stomati prouchousin, araiē d’ eisodos estin,
sentences.l:
There, when into the famous harbour we came, around which a rock,
towering, has come to be unbroken on both sides,
and headlands, thrust forward, facing one another,
at the mouth jut out, and narrow is the entrance,
sentences.i: There, when we came into the famous harbour, around which a towering rock stands unbroken on both sides, and headlands thrust forward, facing one another, jut out at the mouth, and the entrance is narrow,
sentences.n: This long clause has its main verb only in 91, where ἔνθ’ ‘there’ starts again; it is cut at the comma after ἐστιν because the whole sentence runs five lines. ὃν πέρι is ‘around which’: πέρι is Attic περί placed after its word, with the accent thrown back. τετύχηκε is the perfect of τυγχάνω ‘happen to be, be’. ἠλίβατος, ‘towering’, is of unknown meaning: ‘steep, high’ is the traditional guess. διαμπερές is ‘right through, without a break’. ἀκταί are ‘headlands’, προβλῆτες ‘thrust forward’, and προύχουσιν (προέχουσιν) ‘jut out’; ἀλλήλῃσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν, ‘one another’. ἀραιή is ‘narrow’. κλυτόν is the house ‘famous’.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ οἵ γ’ εἴσω πάντες ἔχον νέας ἀμφιελίσσας.
sentences.tr: enth’ hoi g’ eisō pantes echon neas amphielissas.
sentences.l: There they, inside, all held their both-sides-curving ships.
sentences.i: There they all kept their ships, curved on both sides, inside.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ picks up the ἔνθ’ of 87. οἵ γ’ is ‘they’, the other crews, set against ἐγώ ‘I’, who keeps his ship outside at 95: εἴσω ‘inside’ answers ἔξω ‘outside’ there. ἔχον is the unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω, here ‘kept, held’ the ships in place. ἀμφιελίσσας, ‘curved on both sides’, is a stock epithet of ships whose sense is disputed: ‘rowed on both sides’ is the other guess.

sentences.t:
αἱ μὲν ἄρ’ ἔντοσθεν λιμένος κοίλοιο δέδεντο
πλησίαι·
sentences.tr:
hai men ar’ entosthen limenos koiloio dedento
plēsiai·
sentences.l:
They then, inside the hollow harbour, had been bound
close together;
sentences.i: They were moored inside the hollow harbour, close together;
sentences.n: αἱ is the feminine ‘they’, the ships of 91 (νέας is feminine). ἔντοσθεν is ‘inside’, like εἴσω; λιμένος κοίλοιο is ‘the hollow harbour’, with the house ‘hollow’. δέδεντο is the pluperfect passive of δέω ‘bind’, here ‘moor’. πλησίαι is ‘close together’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 93.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ ποτ’ ἀέξετο κῦμά γ’ ἐν αὐτῷ,
οὔτε μέγ’ οὔτ’ ὀλίγον, λευκὴ δ’ ἦν ἀμφὶ γαλήνη·
sentences.tr:
ou men gar pot’ aexeto kyma g’ en autōi,
oute meg’ out’ oligon, leukē d’ ēn amphi galēnē·
sentences.l:
for never did a wave swell in it,
neither great nor small, but white around was a calm;
sentences.i: for no wave ever swelled in it, either great or small, but a white calm lay all round;
sentences.n: This explains why the ships can lie close together: nothing stirs in the harbour. ἀέξετο is the imperfect passive of ἀέξω ‘grow, rise’, and γε in κῦμά γ’ stresses the wave: not even a wave. ἐν αὐτῷ is ‘in it’, the harbour. ἀμφί is an adverb, ‘all round’. λευκή is ‘white’ and also ‘bright’; either suits a still surface. γαλήνη is ‘calm’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν οἶος σχέθον ἔξω νῆα μέλαιναν,
αὐτοῦ ἐπ’ ἐσχατιῇ, πέτρης ἐκ πείσματα δήσας·
sentences.tr:
autar egōn oios schethon exō nēa melainan,
autou ep’ eschatiēi, petrēs ek peismata dēsas·
sentences.l:
But I alone held outside my black ship,
right there at the edge, from a rock having tied cables;
sentences.i: But I alone kept my black ship outside, right there at the edge, after making my cables fast to the rock;
sentences.n: Odysseus separates himself from the rest: this one choice, to stay outside, is what lets his ship escape at 126–127. ἐγών is ἐγώ with a final ν, and οἶος is ‘alone’. σχέθον is an unaugmented aorist of ἔχω, ‘held, kept’, set against ἔχον in 91. αὐτοῦ is ‘right there’ and ἐπ’ ἐσχατιῇ ‘at the edge’. πέτρης ἐκ is ἐκ πέτρης, ‘from a rock’, with the preposition after its noun (anastrophe); πείσματα is ‘cables’ and δήσας ‘having tied’.

sentences.t: ἔστην δὲ σκοπιὴν ἐς παιπαλόεσσαν ἀνελθών.
sentences.tr: estēn de skopiēn es paipaloessan anelthōn.
sentences.l: and I stood, to a rugged lookout having gone up;
sentences.i: and I went up to a rugged lookout and took my stand there;
sentences.n: Odysseus climbs to see the country. ἔστην is ‘I stood’, and ἀνελθών ‘having gone up’. σκοπιή is ‘lookout’ (from σκοπέω ‘look’). παιπαλόεσσαν is the feminine of παιπαλόεις ‘rugged’, a word of uncertain derivation. The line returns at 148 with a comma for its full stop.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μὲν οὔτε βοῶν οὔτ’ ἀνδρῶν φαίνετο ἔργα,
καπνὸν δ’ οἶον ὁρῶμεν ἀπὸ χθονὸς ἀίσσοντα.
sentences.tr:
entha men oute boōn out’ andrōn phaineto erga,
kapnon d’ oion horōmen apo chthonos aissonta.
sentences.l:
There neither of oxen nor of men did works appear,
but smoke only we see darting up from the earth.
sentences.i: There no work of oxen or of men could be seen, but we saw only smoke darting up from the ground.
sentences.n: These lines say what Odysseus sees from the lookout: no sign of work, only smoke. ἔργα βοῶν … ἀνδρῶν is ‘works of oxen and of men’, the work done by oxen and by people. οἶον with the smooth breathing is ‘alone, only’ (οἷον with the rough breathing would be ‘such as’). ὁρῶμεν is a present plural, ‘we see’, in the middle of past narrative, though Odysseus is alone on the lookout; the line gives no reason for the tense or for the plural, and the free English puts it in the past. ἀίσσοντα ‘darting’ is a participle of ἀΐσσω, the verb of ἀίξαντε in 117.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἑτάρους προΐειν πεύθεσθαι ἰόντας,
οἵ τινες ἀνέρες εἶεν ἐπὶ χθονὶ σῖτον ἔδοντες,
ἄνδρε δύω κρίνας, τρίτατον κήρυχ’ ἅμ’ ὀπάσσας.
sentences.tr:
dē tot’ egōn hetarous proïein peuthesthai iontas,
hoi tines aneres eien epi chthoni siton edontes,
andre dyō krinas, tritaton kērych’ ham’ opassas.
sentences.l:
Then I companions sent forth to inquire, going,
who the men might be, on the earth eating bread,
two men choosing, and a third, a herald, along with them adding.
sentences.i: Then I sent some of my companions to go and find out who the men were who ate bread on the earth, choosing two men and adding a herald as a third.
sentences.n: These three lines repeat 9.88–90, where Odysseus sent men to find out who lived among the Lotus-eaters, and the English is the same. ἑτάρους προΐειν πεύθεσθαι ἰόντας is ‘I sent forth companions to inquire, going’; προΐειν is the imperfect of προΐημι. The indirect question has the optative, οἵ τινες ἀνέρες εἶεν, ‘who the men might be’, and σῖτον ἔδοντες ‘eating bread’ means that they live on grain. ἄνδρε δύω is a dual, ‘two men’; τρίτατον is ‘as a third’, and ὀπάσσας ‘adding’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἴσαν ἐκβάντες λείην ὁδόν, ᾗ περ ἄμαξαι
ἄστυδ’ ἀφ’ ὑψηλῶν ὀρέων καταγίνεον ὕλην,
κούρῃ δὲ ξύμβληντο πρὸ ἄστεος ὑδρευούσῃ,
θυγατέρ’ ἰφθίμῃ Λαιστρυγόνος Ἀντιφάταο.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ isan ekbantes leiēn hodon, hēi per amaxai
astyd’ aph’ hypsēlōn oreōn katagineon hylēn,
kourēi de xymblēnto pro asteos hydreuousēi,
thygater’ iphthimēi Laistrygonos Antiphatao.
sentences.l:
And they went, having disembarked, along a smooth road, by which wagons
to the town from high mountains were bringing down wood,
and a maiden they met before the town, drawing water,
a daughter, mighty, of Antiphates the Laestrygonian.
sentences.i: They disembarked and went along a smooth road, the one by which the wagons used to bring wood down to the town from the high mountains, and they met a girl in front of the town, drawing water, a mighty daughter of Antiphates the Laestrygonian.
sentences.n: Line 106 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of θυγατέρ’, short by nature, is lengthened to fill the long place of the first foot. οἱ δ’ is ‘they’; ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘went’, and ἐκβάντες ‘having disembarked’. ᾗ περ is ‘by which very way’, and ἄστυδ’ has the -δε of motion, ‘to the town’; ὕλην is ‘wood’, brought down by wagons (ἄμαξαι) on καταγίνεον, an uncontracted imperfect of καταγινέω (Attic κατάγω). ξύμβληντο is an aorist middle of συμβάλλω ‘meet’, with the dative κούρῃ; ὑδρευούσῃ is a participle of ὑδρεύω ‘draw water’. θυγατέρ’ is best read as the dative θυγατέρι with its ι elided, agreeing with κούρῃ and ἰφθίμῃ (‘mighty’).

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐς κρήνην κατεβήσετο καλλιρέεθρον
Ἀρτακίην·
sentences.tr:
hē men ar’ es krēnēn katebēseto kallireethron
Artakiēn·
sentences.l:
She then to the spring went down, fair-flowing,
Artacia;
sentences.i: She went down to the fair-flowing spring Artacia;
sentences.n: ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ is ‘she, for her part’, answered by οἱ δὲ in 109: while she goes down to the spring, the men go up to her. κατεβήσετο is an aorist middle of καταβαίνω in -σε-, ‘went down’. καλλιρέεθρον is ‘fair-flowing’ (καλλι- ‘fair’; ῥέεθρον ‘stream’), and Ἀρτακίην is the spring’s name. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 108.

sentences.t: ἔνθεν γὰρ ὕδωρ προτὶ ἄστυ φέρεσκον·
sentences.tr: enthen gar hydōr proti asty phereskon·
sentences.l: for from there water to the town they used to carry;
sentences.i: for it was from there that they used to carry water to the town;
sentences.n: γάρ says why the girl is at this spring: the town draws its water here. φέρεσκον is an iterative imperfect, with the suffix -σκ- giving ‘used to carry’, and its ‘they’ is the townspeople, who are not named. προτί is πρός ‘to’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ παριστάμενοι προσεφώνεον ἔκ τ’ ἐρέοντο
ὅς τις τῶνδ’ εἴη βασιλεὺς καὶ οἷσιν ἀνάσσοι·
sentences.tr:
hoi de paristamenoi prosephōneon ek t’ ereonto
hos tis tōnd’ eiē basileus kai hoisin anassoi·
sentences.l:
And they, standing beside, spoke to her and asked out
who of these might be king and over whom he might rule;
sentences.i: And they stood beside her, spoke to her, and asked who among these people was king and over whom he ruled;
sentences.n: The men question her as strangers. παριστάμενοι is ‘standing beside’ and προσεφώνεον ‘spoke to’; ἔκ τ’ ἐρέοντο is ἐξερέοντο, tmesis, ‘asked out’. The indirect question has the optative, as at 101: ὅς τις τῶνδ’ εἴη βασιλεύς is ‘who of these might be king’, and οἷσιν ἀνάσσοι ‘over whom he might rule’, a dative after ἀνάσσω. τῶνδε is ‘of these’, the people of the town. No quotation marks are needed: the question is reported.

sentences.t: ἡ δὲ μάλ’ αὐτίκα πατρὸς ἐπέφραδεν ὑψερεφὲς δῶ.
sentences.tr: hē de mal’ autika patros epephraden hypserephes dō.
sentences.l: And she very promptly of her father pointed out the high-roofed house.
sentences.i: And she at once pointed out her father’s high-roofed house.
sentences.n: She answers by pointing, not by speaking: the house of her father is the answer to the question about the king. ἐπέφραδεν is an aorist of ἐπιφράζω ‘point out’. δῶ is a short form of δῶμα ‘house’, and ὑψερεφές is ‘high-roofed’, the house word. μάλ’ αὐτίκα is ‘very promptly’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐπεὶ εἰσῆλθον κλυτὰ δώματα, τὴν δὲ γυναῖκα
εὗρον, ὅσην τ’ ὄρεος κορυφήν, κατὰ δ’ ἔστυγον αὐτήν.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ epei eisēlthon klyta dōmata, tēn de gynaika
heuron, hosēn t’ oreos koryphēn, kata d’ estygon autēn.
sentences.l:
And they, when they entered the famous halls, the woman
found, as large as a mountain’s peak, and utterly loathed her.
sentences.i: And when they entered the famous halls, they found the woman as big as a mountain peak, and were filled with loathing for her.
sentences.n: τὴν δὲ γυναῖκα is ‘the woman’, the king’s wife, who is not named: the δέ opens the main clause after the ἐπεί clause. κλυτὰ δώματα is ‘the famous halls’, with the house word. ὅσην τ’ ὄρεος κορυφήν is ‘as large as a mountain’s peak’, with the epic τε and ὄρεος, the uncontracted genitive of ὄρος. κατὰ … ἔστυγον is tmesis for the verb ‘loathe’, the preverb strengthening it; αὐτήν is ‘her’.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ αἶψ’ ἐξ ἀγορῆς ἐκάλει κλυτὸν Ἀντιφατῆα,
ὃν πόσιν, ὃς δὴ τοῖσιν ἐμήσατο λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ aips’ ex agorēs ekalei klyton Antiphatēa,
hon posin, hos dē toisin emēsato lygron olethron.
sentences.l:
And she at once from the assembly called famous Antiphates,
her own husband, who indeed for them devised grievous destruction.
sentences.i: She at once called famous Antiphates, her own husband, from the assembly, the very man who devised grievous destruction for them.
sentences.n: ὃν πόσιν has ὅν as the possessive, ‘her own’, not the relative; the relative is the ὅς that follows in the same line. ἐξ ἀγορῆς is ‘from the assembly’ (the meeting or the place of meeting), and κλυτὸν Ἀντιφατῆα is ‘famous Antiphates’, with the accusative in -ῆα. ἐμήσατο is the aorist middle of μήδομαι ‘devise’, τοῖσιν is ‘for them’, and λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον is ‘grievous destruction’; δή marks him as the man who did it.

sentences.t: αὐτίχ’ ἕνα μάρψας ἑτάρων ὡπλίσσατο δεῖπνον·
sentences.tr: autich’ hena marpsas hetarōn hōplissato deipnon·
sentences.l: At once one seizing of the companions he made ready a meal;
sentences.i: At once he seized one of my companions and prepared himself a meal;
sentences.n: The subject is Antiphates, called in 114 and not named again. The poem says it plainly: he prepares a meal from one of the men. μάρψας is the aorist participle of μάρπτω ‘seize’, ἑτάρων a partitive genitive, and ὡπλίσσατο the aorist middle of ὁπλίζω ‘make ready’, with the sense ‘for himself’. δεῖπνον is ‘meal’.

sentences.t: τὼ δὲ δύ’ ἀίξαντε φυγῇ ἐπὶ νῆας ἱκέσθην.
sentences.tr: tō de dy’ aixante phygēi epi nēas hikesthēn.
sentences.l: but the two, darting away, in flight to the ships arrived.
sentences.i: but the other two darted away and reached the ships in flight.
sentences.n: The pair who escape are the other two of the three sent out in 100–102. τώ is the dual of the pronoun, ‘those two’, and ἀίξαντε and ἱκέσθην are dual too: ἀίξαντε the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’ (see 99), and ἱκέσθην the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘arrive’. φυγῇ is ‘in flight’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὁ τεῦχε βοὴν διὰ ἄστεος·
sentences.tr: autar ho teuche boēn dia asteos·
sentences.l: but he was making a shout through the town;
sentences.i: but he raised a shout through the town;
sentences.n: ὁ is Antiphates. τεῦχε is the unaugmented imperfect of τεύχω ‘make’; with βοήν ‘shout’ it is ‘raise a cry’. ἄστεος is the genitive of ἄστυ, with διά ‘through’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 118.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἀίοντες
φοίτων ἴφθιμοι Λαιστρυγόνες ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος,
μυρίοι, οὐκ ἄνδρεσσιν ἐοικότες, ἀλλὰ Γίγασιν.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ aiontes
phoitōn iphthimoi Laistrygones allothen allos,
myrioi, ouk andressin eoikotes, alla Gigasin.
sentences.l:
and they, hearing,
were coming in, mighty Laestrygonians, each from another place,
countless, not like men, but like Giants.
sentences.i: and when they heard it they came crowding in from every side, mighty Laestrygonians, countless, not like men but like Giants.
sentences.n: The Laestrygonians arrive in crowds, and Homer compares them to Giants (Γίγασιν), the savage race the Phaeacians name at 7.206. οἱ δ’ is ‘and they’; ἀίοντες is ‘hearing’; φοίτων is the imperfect of φοιτάω ‘come and go, throng’. ἴφθιμοι is ‘mighty’, as always. ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος is ‘each from another place’. μυρίοι is ‘countless’, literally ‘ten thousand’. ἄνδρεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσιν, and ἐοικότες, the perfect participle of ἔοικα, takes the dative: ‘like men’, ‘like Giants’.

sentences.t:
οἵ ῥ’ ἀπὸ πετράων ἀνδραχθέσι χερμαδίοισιν
βάλλον·
sentences.tr:
hoi rh’ apo petraōn andrachthesi chermadioisin
ballon·
sentences.l:
These then from the rocks with man-burdening stones
were pelting;
sentences.i: They pelted us from the rocks with stones as heavy as a man could carry;
sentences.n: οἵ ῥ’ is οἱ ῥα ‘they then’, the Laestrygonians, now on the cliffs round the harbour. ἀνδραχθέσι, from ἀνήρ ‘man’ and ἄχθος ‘burden’, is ‘as heavy as a man can carry’, and χερμαδίοισιν is ‘stones’ (for throwing); πετράων is the genitive plural in -άων. βάλλον ‘were pelting’ has no object in the Greek, which the free English supplies. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 122.

sentences.t:
ἄφαρ δὲ κακὸς κόναβος κατὰ νῆας ὀρώρει
ἀνδρῶν τ’ ὀλλυμένων νηῶν θ’ ἅμα ἀγνυμενάων·
sentences.tr:
aphar de kakos konabos kata nēas orōrei
andrōn t’ ollymenōn nēōn th’ hama agnymenaōn·
sentences.l:
and at once an evil din along the ships had risen
of men perishing and of ships together being broken;
sentences.i: and at once a terrible din rose up among the ships, of men perishing and ships being smashed at the same time;
sentences.n: ἄφαρ is ‘at once’. ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι ‘had risen’, used for ‘arose’. κόναβος is ‘din, crash’, and κακός, here ‘evil’, makes it a dreadful one. The two genitives ἀνδρῶν ὀλλυμένων and νηῶν ἀγνυμενάων depend on κόναβος: ὀλλυμένων is a present passive participle ‘perishing’, and ἀγνυμενάων an uncontracted genitive plural of ἄγνυμι ‘break’ (Attic ἀγνυμένων); θ’ ἅμα is ‘and at the same time’.

sentences.t: ἰχθῦς δ’ ὣς πείροντες ἀτερπέα δαῖτα φέροντο.
sentences.tr: ichthys d’ hōs peirontes aterpea daita pheronto.
sentences.l: and, like fish, piercing them, a joyless feast they carried off.
sentences.i: and, piercing them like fish, they carried off a joyless feast.
sentences.n: The poem does not turn away: the feast is the men themselves. ἰχθῦς δ’ ὣς is ‘and like fish’, with ὥς ‘as, like’ after its noun. πείροντες is ‘piercing’ (πείρω ‘pierce through’), and the subject is still the Laestrygonians. ἀτερπέα is ‘joyless’ (ἀ- ‘not’ and τέρπω ‘delight’), said from the victims’ side; δαῖτα is ‘feast’, φέροντο the imperfect middle ‘carried off for themselves’.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ οἱ τοὺς ὄλεκον λιμένος πολυβενθέος ἐντός,
τόφρα δ’ ἐγὼ ξίφος ὀξὺ ἐρυσσάμενος παρὰ μηροῦ
τῷ ἀπὸ πείσματ’ ἔκοψα νεὸς κυανοπρῴροιο.
sentences.tr:
ophr’ hoi tous olekon limenos polybentheos entos,
tophra d’ egō xiphos oxy eryssamenos para mērou
tōi apo peismat’ ekopsa neos kyanoprōiroio.
sentences.l:
While they were killing those within the very deep harbour,
meanwhile I, my sharp sword drawing from beside my thigh,
with it I cut off the cables of the dark-prowed ship.
sentences.i: While they were killing the men inside the deep harbour, I drew my sharp sword from beside my thigh and with it cut the cables of my dark-prowed ship.
sentences.n: ὄφρα … τόφρα is ‘while … meanwhile’, setting the killing against Odysseus’s one act: he cuts his ship loose at once because it alone is tied to the rock outside (95–96). οἱ τοὺς ὄλεκον is ‘they were killing those’, ὄλεκον an imperfect of ὀλέκω; πολυβενθέος is ‘very deep’ (πολυ- ‘very’, βένθος ‘depth’), and ἐντός ‘inside’. ξίφος ὀξύ is ‘sharp sword’, ἐρυσσάμενος ‘drawing’, and παρὰ μηροῦ ‘from beside the thigh’. ἀπὸ … ἔκοψα is tmesis, ‘cut off’, and κυανοπρῴροιο ‘dark-prowed’ is a genitive in -οιο.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δ’ ἐμοῖς ἑτάροισιν ἐποτρύνας ἐκέλευσα
ἐμβαλέειν κώπῃς, ἵν’ ὑπὲκ κακότητα φύγοιμεν·
sentences.tr:
aipsa d’ emois hetaroisin epotrynas ekeleusa
embaleein kōpēis, hin’ hypek kakotēta phygoimen·
sentences.l:
And at once my companions, having urged on, I ordered
to throw themselves upon the oars, that out of harm we might flee;
sentences.i: At once I urged my companions on and ordered them to throw themselves upon the oars, so that we might escape from our trouble;
sentences.n: Line 129 is 9.489 word for word, and its English is the same. ἐμοῖς ἑτάροισιν is a dative with ἐκέλευσα ‘I ordered’, and ἐποτρύνας ‘having urged on’. ἐμβαλέειν κώπῃς is an uncontracted infinitive (Attic ἐμβαλεῖν) with a dative plural in -ῃς: ‘to throw themselves upon the oars’. ἵν’ … φύγοιμεν is a purpose clause with the optative, and ὑπέκ is ‘out from under’ with the accusative κακότητα ‘harm, trouble’.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἅλα πάντες ἀνέρριψαν, δείσαντες ὄλεθρον.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ hala pantes anerripsan, deisantes olethron.
sentences.l: And they the salt-sea all tossed up, fearing destruction.
sentences.i: and in fear of destruction they all tossed up the salt sea.
sentences.n: The oars of 129 are meant, though the Greek does not name them: rowing hard tosses the water up. ἀνέρριψαν is the aorist of ἀναρρίπτω ‘throw up’, and ἅλα is ‘the salt-sea’. δείσαντες is the aorist participle of δείδω ‘fear’, with the accusative ὄλεθρον ‘destruction’.

sentences.t:
ἀσπασίως δ’ ἐς πόντον ἐπηρεφέας φύγε πέτρας
νηῦς ἐμή·
sentences.tr:
aspasiōs d’ es ponton epērepheas phyge petras
nēus emē·
sentences.l:
And gladly into the open-sea fled the overhanging rocks
my ship;
sentences.i: And with joy my ship fled the overhanging rocks into the open sea;
sentences.n: φύγε is an unaugmented aorist of φεύγω, and the thing fled is the accusative πέτρας: the ship escapes the rocks that close in on the harbour mouth and comes out to sea. ἀσπασίως is ‘gladly’; ἐπηρεφέας, ‘overhanging’, is an accusative plural of ἐπηρεφής (cf. ἐπερέφω ‘roof over’). The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 132.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ αἱ ἄλλαι ἀολλέες αὐτόθ’ ὄλοντο.
sentences.tr: autar hai allai aollees autoth’ olonto.
sentences.l: but the others, all together, right there perished.
sentences.i: but all the others perished there together.
sentences.n: αἱ ἄλλαι is feminine, ‘the others’, the other ships; ἀολλέες ‘all together’ has one form for masculine and feminine, so it can go with the ships or with the crews aboard them, and the sentence does not choose: ships and crews are lost as one. αὐτόθ’ is αὐτόθι ‘right there’. ὄλοντο is the unaugmented aorist middle of ὄλλυμι ‘perish’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν δὲ προτέρω πλέομεν ἀκαχήμενοι ἦτορ,
ἄσμενοι ἐκ θανάτοιο, φίλους ὀλέσαντες ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr:
enthen de proterō pleomen akachēmenoi ētor,
asmenoi ek thanatoio, philous olesantes hetairous.
sentences.l:
From there farther we sailed, grieved in heart,
glad to be out of death, dear companions having lost.
sentences.i: From there we sailed on, grieved at heart, glad to be out of death, though we had lost our dear companions.
sentences.n: These two lines are 9.62–63 word for word, and the first is also 77; the English is as shipped. Here the lines fit exactly: the crews of all the other ships have just perished (132), and the one ship that survives is glad to be out of death. ἄσμενοι is ‘glad’, ἐκ θανάτοιο ‘out of death’ with a genitive in -οιο, and φίλους ὀλέσαντες ἑταίρους ‘having lost dear companions’. A new paragraph begins.

sentences.t: Αἰαίην δ’ ἐς νῆσον ἀφικόμεθ’·
sentences.tr: Aiaiēn d’ es nēson aphikometh’·
sentences.l: And to the Aeaean island we came;
sentences.i: We came to the island of Aeaea;
sentences.n: Αἰαίην is the adjective ‘Aeaean’, ‘of Aeaea’, agreeing with νῆσον; it names Circe’s island, as Αἰαίη did Circe herself at 9.32. ἀφικόμεθ’ is ἀφικόμεθα, the aorist of ἀφικνέομαι ‘arrive’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 135, before the description of who lives there.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἔναιε
Κίρκη ἐυπλόκαμος, δεινὴ θεὸς αὐδήεσσα,
αὐτοκασιγνήτη ὀλοόφρονος Αἰήταο·
sentences.tr:
entha d’ enaie
Kirkē eyplokamos, deinē theos audēessa,
autokasignētē oloophronos Aiētao·
sentences.i: and there lived fine-plaited Circe, a dread goddess who speaks with a human voice, own sister of baleful-minded Aeetes;
sentences.n: Circe is introduced with her stock epithets, translated here as they will be each time. ἐυπλόκαμος is ‘fine-plaited’, the word used of Calypso and of Dawn. δεινὴ θεὸς αὐδήεσσα is ‘a dread goddess endowed with speech’; αὐδήεσσα means ‘having a voice’, and the ancient explanation is that she talks as mortals do, though the force of the word is debated. αὐτοκασιγνήτη is ‘own sister’, born of the same parents, as 138–139 say, and ὀλοόφρων is ‘baleful-minded’ (ὀλοός ‘destructive’, φρήν ‘mind’), as of Atlas at 1.52. ἔναιε is the imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’ (its ἐ- is the augment); Αἰήταο is a genitive in -αο.

sentences.t:
ἄμφω δ’ ἐκγεγάτην φαεσιμβρότου Ἠελίοιο
μητρός τ’ ἐκ Πέρσης, τὴν Ὠκεανὸς τέκε παῖδα.
sentences.tr:
amphō d’ ekgegatēn phaesimbrotou Ēelioio
mētros t’ ek Persēs, tēn Ōkeanos teke paida.
sentences.l:
and both were born of the mortal-lighting Sun
and of a mother, Perse, whom Oceanus begot as his child.
sentences.i: and both were born of the Sun, who gives light to mortals, and of their mother Perse, whom Oceanus begot as his child.
sentences.n: Circe and Aeetes have the same two parents. ἄμφω is the dual ‘both’, and ἐκγεγάτην the dual perfect of ἐκγίγνομαι ‘be born from’. φαεσιμβρότου, ‘giving light to mortals’ (φάος ‘light’, βροτός ‘mortal’), is a standing epithet of the Sun, whose name Ἠελίοιο is a genitive in -οιο; he is the father. μητρός τ’ ἐκ Πέρσης is ‘and from a mother, Perse’, and τέκε is the unaugmented aorist ‘begot’, of Oceanus (Ὠκεανός), who is Perse’s father; παῖδα is ‘as his child’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἐπ’ ἀκτῆς νηὶ κατηγαγόμεσθα σιωπῇ
ναύλοχον ἐς λιμένα, καί τις θεὸς ἡγεμόνευεν.
sentences.tr:
entha d’ ep’ aktēs nēi katēgagomestha siōpēi
naulochon es limena, kai tis theos hēgemoneuen.
sentences.l:
And there to the shore in the ship we put in, in silence,
into a harbour fit for ships, and some god was leading the way.
sentences.i: There we put in to the shore with our ship, in silence, into a harbour where ships can lie, and some god was guiding us.
sentences.n: The crew comes into harbour in silence, and a god, unnamed, shows the way. κατηγαγόμεσθα, with -μεσθα for -μεθα, is the aorist middle of κατάγω, the sailor’s word for bringing a ship in to land: ‘we put in’. νηί is the dative of ναῦς, ‘with the ship’, and σιωπῇ ‘in silence’. ναύλοχον is ‘fit for ships’, as at 4.846, and ἡγεμόνευεν ‘was guiding, was leading the way’; καί τις θεός is ‘and some god’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα τότ’ ἐκβάντες δύο τ’ ἤματα καὶ δύο νύκτας
κείμεθ’ ὁμοῦ καμάτῳ τε καὶ ἄλγεσι θυμὸν ἔδοντες.
sentences.tr:
entha tot’ ekbantes dyo t’ ēmata kai dyo nyktas
keimeth’ homou kamatōi te kai algesi thymon edontes.
sentences.l:
There then, having disembarked, two days and two nights
we lay, together with weariness and with pains eating our hearts.
sentences.i: There we went ashore and lay for two days and two nights, eating our hearts out with weariness and pain.
sentences.n: Line 143 is 9.75, and its English follows the shipped unit; θυμὸν ἔδοντες, ‘eating our hearts’, is the idiom for wasting away with distress. ἐκβάντες is ‘having disembarked’; δύο τ’ ἤματα καὶ δύο νύκτας are accusatives of duration; κείμεθ’ is κείμεθα, the imperfect of κεῖμαι ‘we lay’. ὁμοῦ is ‘together with’ the datives καμάτῳ ‘weariness’ and ἄλγεσι ‘pains’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τρίτον ἦμαρ ἐυπλόκαμος τέλεσ’ Ἠώς,
καὶ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἐμὸν ἔγχος ἑλὼν καὶ φάσγανον ὀξὺ
καρπαλίμως παρὰ νηὸς ἀνήιον ἐς περιωπήν,
εἴ πως ἔργα ἴδοιμι βροτῶν ἐνοπήν τε πυθοίμην.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē triton ēmar eyplokamos teles’ Ēōs,
kai tot’ egōn emon enchos helōn kai phasganon oxy
karpalimōs para nēos anēion es periōpēn,
ei pōs erga idoimi brotōn enopēn te pythoimēn.
sentences.l:
But when indeed the third day fine-plaited Dawn brought to its end,
then I, my spear taking and my sharp sword,
quickly from beside the ship went up to a vantage-point,
if somehow works I might see of mortals and a voice I might learn of.
sentences.i: But when fine-plaited Dawn had brought the third day round, then I took my spear and my sharp sword and quickly went up from beside the ship to a vantage-point, to see if I could somehow catch sight of the works of mortals and hear a voice.
sentences.n: Line 144 is 5.390, with the same English: the third day since the landing at 142. Odysseus arms himself and climbs to find out who lives here. ἐγών is ἐγώ with a final ν; ἔγχος is ‘spear’ and φάσγανον ὀξύ ‘sharp sword’. ἀνήιον is the imperfect of ἄνειμι ‘go up’, and καρπαλίμως ‘quickly’. περιωπή is a place from which one looks all round, ‘a vantage-point’ (compare σκοπιή ‘lookout’, 97). εἴ πως with the optatives ἴδοιμι and πυθοίμην is ‘in the hope that I might somehow see … and learn’; ἔργα βροτῶν is ‘works of mortals’ and ἐνοπή ‘voice, cry’.

sentences.t:
ἔστην δὲ σκοπιὴν ἐς παιπαλόεσσαν ἀνελθών,
καί μοι ἐείσατο καπνὸς ἀπὸ χθονὸς εὐρυοδείης,
Κίρκης ἐν μεγάροισι, διὰ δρυμὰ πυκνὰ καὶ ὕλην.
sentences.tr:
estēn de skopiēn es paipaloessan anelthōn,
kai moi eeisato kapnos apo chthonos euryodeiēs,
Kirkēs en megaroisi, dia dryma pykna kai hylēn.
sentences.l:
And I stood, to a rugged lookout having gone up,
and to me appeared smoke from the wide-wayed earth,
in Circe’s halls, through thick coppices and woodland.
sentences.i: And I went up to a rugged lookout and took my stand there, and smoke appeared to me from the wide-wayed earth, in Circe’s halls, through thick coppices and woodland.
sentences.n: Line 148 is 97 again, except that its full stop becomes a comma. ἐείσατο is the aorist of εἴδομαι ‘appear’, with the dative μοι. χθονὸς εὐρυοδείης is ‘the wide-wayed earth’, the stock phrase kept as it always is. Κίρκης ἐν μεγάροισι is ‘in Circe’s halls’ (μέγαρα is a plural for one dwelling): the smoke comes from her house. δρυμά is ‘coppices, thickets’, and ὕλη ‘woodland’; πυκνά is ‘thick’.

sentences.t:
μερμήριξα δ’ ἔπειτα κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμὸν
ἐλθεῖν ἠδὲ πυθέσθαι, ἐπεὶ ἴδον αἴθοπα καπνόν.
sentences.tr:
mermērixa d’ epeita kata phrena kai kata thymon
elthein ēde pythesthai, epei idon aithopa kapnon.
sentences.l:
And I pondered then in mind and in heart
to go and to inquire, since I had seen the fire-faced smoke.
sentences.i: Then in my mind and heart I debated whether to go and find out, since I had seen the smoke that has the look of fire.
sentences.n: μερμήριξα with the infinitives ἐλθεῖν ἠδὲ πυθέσθαι is ‘I debated whether to go and find out’; the matter is settled in the next lines. κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν is the stock ‘in mind and in heart’. ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist ‘I saw’. αἴθοπα καπνόν is ‘fire-faced smoke’: αἴθοψ, from αἴθω ‘burn’ and ὄψ ‘face, look’, is the word used of wine, ‘the wine that has the look of fire’, and is built the same way.

sentences.t:
ὧδε δέ μοι φρονέοντι δοάσσατο κέρδιον εἶναι,
πρῶτ’ ἐλθόντ’ ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν καὶ θῖνα θαλάσσης
δεῖπνον ἑταίροισιν δόμεναι προέμεν τε πυθέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
hōde de moi phroneonti doassato kerdion einai,
prōt’ elthont’ epi nēa thoēn kai thina thalassēs
deipnon hetairoisin domenai proemen te pythesthai.
sentences.l:
And thus to me considering it seemed better to be,
first going to the swift ship and the shore of the sea
a meal to my companions to give and to send forth to inquire.
sentences.i: And this, as I thought it over, seemed to me the better course: to go first to the swift ship and the shore of the sea, give my companions a meal, and send them forth to inquire.
sentences.n: δοάσσατο κέρδιον εἶναι is ‘it seemed better’, as at 5.474 and 6.145; δοάσσατο is an aorist ‘seemed’, and κέρδιον the comparative of κέρδος ‘gain, advantage’. φρονέοντι is the uncontracted participle, dative with μοι: ‘to me thinking’. The infinitives δόμεναι ‘to give’ (Attic δοῦναι) and προέμεν ‘to send forth’ (Attic προεῖναι) are in -μεναι and -έμεν, and πυθέσθαι is ‘to inquire’; ἐλθόντ’ is accusative, agreeing with the unspoken ‘me’ who is to do these things. νῆα θοήν is the stock ‘swift ship’, and θῖνα θαλάσσης ‘the shore of the sea’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦα κιὼν νεὸς ἀμφιελίσσης,
καὶ τότε τίς με θεῶν ὀλοφύρατο μοῦνον ἐόντα,
ὅς ῥά μοι ὑψίκερων ἔλαφον μέγαν εἰς ὁδὸν αὐτὴν
ἧκεν.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē schedon ēa kiōn neos amphielissēs,
kai tote tis me theōn olophyrato mounon eonta,
hos rha moi hypsikerōn elaphon megan eis hodon autēn
hēken.
sentences.l:
But when indeed near I was going to the both-sides-curving ship,
then some one of the gods me pitied, being alone,
who for me a high-horned stag, great, into my very path
sent.
sentences.i: But when I was drawing near the ship, curved on both sides, then one of the gods took pity on me, alone as I was, and sent a great high-horned stag into my very path.
sentences.n: A god takes pity on Odysseus and sends him food; the god is not named. ἦα is the epic imperfect of εἶμι ‘I was going’, with κιών ‘going’; σχεδὸν νεὸς is ‘near the ship’, with the genitive. τίς με θεῶν ὀλοφύρατο is ‘some one of the gods pitied me’, μοῦνον ἐόντα ‘being alone’. ὑψίκερων is ‘high-horned’ (ὑψι- ‘high’, κέρας ‘horn’), and ἔλαφον is ‘stag’; ὅς ῥά μοι … ἧκεν is ‘who then sent for me’, from ἵημι. ἀμφιελίσσης is ‘curved on both sides’, as at 91. The sentence ends at the full stop in the middle of 159.

sentences.t:
ὁ μὲν ποταμόνδε κατήιεν ἐκ νομοῦ ὕλης
πιόμενος·
sentences.tr:
ho men potamonde katēien ek nomou hylēs
piomenos·
sentences.l:
He to the river was coming down from the pasture of the wood
to drink;
sentences.i: He was coming down to the river from his pasture in the wood, to drink;
sentences.n: ὁ μέν is ‘he’, the stag, now the subject. ποταμόνδε is ‘to the river’, with -δε of motion; κατήιεν is the imperfect of κάτειμι ‘was coming down’. νομοῦ ὕλης is ‘the pasture of the wood’ (νομός ‘pasture, grazing’). πιόμενος is the future participle of πίνω, ‘to drink’, of purpose. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 160.

sentences.t: δὴ γάρ μιν ἔχεν μένος ἠελίοιο.
sentences.tr: dē gar min echen menos ēelioio.
sentences.l: for indeed him held the strength of the sun.
sentences.i: for the strength of the sun had hold of him.
sentences.n: δὴ γάρ gives the reason the stag comes to drink. μιν is an epic ‘him’, and ἔχεν is the unaugmented imperfect ‘held’. μένος ἠελίοιο is ‘the strength of the sun’ (μένος is the house ‘strength’), that is its heat; ἠελίοιο is a genitive in -οιο of ἠέλιος ‘sun’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἐγὼ ἐκβαίνοντα κατ’ ἄκνηστιν μέσα νῶτα
πλῆξα·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ egō ekbainonta kat’ aknēstin mesa nōta
plēxa·
sentences.l:
And him I, as he was coming out, along the spine, the middle of the back,
struck;
sentences.i: As he came out, I struck him along the spine, in the middle of the back;
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ἐγώ … πλῆξα is ‘and him I struck’, the aorist of πλήσσω. ἐκβαίνοντα is ‘coming out’; the Greek does not say out of what. ἄκνηστις is the spine, and κατ’ ἄκνηστιν ‘along the spine’; μέσα νῶτα is ‘the middle of the back’, with a plural noun for one back. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 162.

sentences.t:
τὸ δ’ ἀντικρὺ δόρυ χάλκεον ἐξεπέρησε,
κὰδ δ’ ἔπεσ’ ἐν κονίῃσι μακών, ἀπὸ δ’ ἔπτατο θυμός.
sentences.tr:
to d’ antikry dory chalkeon exeperēse,
kad d’ epes’ en koniēisi makōn, apo d’ eptato thymos.
sentences.l:
and straight through the bronze spear passed out;
and down he fell in the dust, crying out, and away flew his life.
sentences.i: and the bronze spear passed clean through him and out; he fell down in the dust with a cry, and his life flew away.
sentences.n: τό is the article before δόρυ, ‘the spear’; ἀντικρύ is ‘straight through’ and ἐξεπέρησε the aorist of ἐκπεράω ‘pass out through’. κὰδ … ἔπεσ’ is tmesis for κατέπεσε ‘fell down’, κὰδ being κατά assimilated to the δ that follows, and ἀπὸ … ἔπτατο tmesis for ‘flew away’. μακών is the aorist participle of μηκάομαι, the cry an animal makes. ἐν κονίῃσι is a dative plural, ‘in the dust’. θυμός here is the life that leaves the body, not the seat of feeling, so it is ‘life’ and not the house ‘heart’.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἐγὼ ἐμβαίνων δόρυ χάλκεον ἐξ ὠτειλῆς
εἰρυσάμην·
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ egō embainōn dory chalkeon ex ōteilēs
eirysamēn·
sentences.l:
And on him I, stepping, the bronze spear out of the wound
drew out;
sentences.i: and, setting my foot on him, I drew the bronze spear out of the wound;
sentences.n: τῷ is the stag, a dative with ἐμβαίνων ‘stepping on’. εἰρυσάμην is an aorist middle of ἐρύω ‘draw’, and ἐξ ὠτειλῆς is ‘out of the wound’ (ὠτειλή ‘wound’). The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 165.

sentences.t:
τὸ μὲν αὖθι κατακλίνας ἐπὶ γαίῃ
εἴασ’·
sentences.tr:
to men authi kataklinas epi gaiēi
eias’·
sentences.l:
it there, having laid down upon the ground,
I left;
sentences.i: I laid it down there on the ground and left it;
sentences.n: τὸ μέν is the spear, ‘it, for my part’, and the contrast comes with αὐτὰρ ἐγώ in the next unit: the spear stays on the ground while Odysseus does something else. κατακλίνας is ‘having laid down’, αὖθι ‘there, on the spot’, and εἴασ’ is εἴασα, the aorist of ἐάω ‘let be, leave’. The unit begins and ends in the middle of a line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ σπασάμην ῥῶπάς τε λύγους τε,
πεῖσμα δ’, ὅσον τ’ ὄργυιαν, ἐυστρεφὲς ἀμφοτέρωθεν
πλεξάμενος συνέδησα πόδας δεινοῖο πελώρου,
sentences.tr:
autar egō spasamēn rhōpas te lygous te,
peisma d’, hoson t’ orguian, eystrephes amphoterōthen
plexamenos synedēsa podas deinoio pelōrou,
sentences.l:
but I pulled up twigs and withies,
and a rope, as much as a fathom, well-twisted from both sides,
having plaited, I bound together the feet of the dread monster,
sentences.i: But I pulled up twigs and withies, plaited a rope about a fathom long, well twisted from both sides, and bound together the feet of the dread monster,
sentences.n: The unit stops at the comma after πελώρου because the sentence runs from 166 to 171, six lines. σπασάμην is the aorist middle of σπάω ‘pull’; ῥῶπας are ‘twigs’ and λύγους ‘withies’, pliant shoots, which are presumably the stuff of the rope, though the Greek does not say so. πεῖσμα is ‘rope’ and πλεξάμενος ‘having plaited’; ὅσον τ’ ὄργυιαν is ‘as much as a fathom’, the stretch of the outstretched arms, about six feet. ἐυστρεφές is ‘well-twisted’, and ἀμφοτέρωθεν ‘from both sides’. συνέδησα is ‘I bound together’, and δεινοῖο πελώρου, a genitive in -οιο, is ‘of the dread monster’: πέλωρ ‘monster’ is the noun behind πελώριος ‘monstrous’ at 9.187.

sentences.t:
βῆν δὲ καταλοφάδεια φέρων ἐπὶ νῆα μέλαιναν
ἔγχει ἐρειδόμενος, ἐπεὶ οὔ πως ἦεν ἐπ’ ὤμου
χειρὶ φέρειν ἑτέρῃ·
sentences.tr:
bēn de katalophadeia pherōn epi nēa melainan
enchei ereidomenos, epei ou pōs ēen ep’ ōmou
cheiri pherein heterēi·
sentences.i: and I went to the black ship, carrying it slung across my neck and leaning on my spear, since there was no way to carry it on my shoulder with one hand;
sentences.n: βῆν is the unaugmented aorist ‘I went’, the first person of the verb in βῆ δ’ ἴμεν. καταλοφάδεια is an adverb from λόφος ‘neck, nape’: the beast, its feet tied at 168, hangs over his neck. ἔγχει ἐρειδόμενος is ‘leaning on my spear’, with the dative of what he leans on. ἦεν is the epic imperfect of εἰμί, here impersonal, ‘it was possible’, with the infinitive φέρειν, and ἑτέρῃ is ‘the other (hand)’: one hand is busy with the spear. νῆα μέλαιναν is ‘the black ship’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 171.

sentences.t: μάλα γὰρ μέγα θηρίον ἦεν.
sentences.tr: mala gar mega thērion ēen.
sentences.l: for very great a beast it was.
sentences.i: for it was a very big beast.
sentences.n: γάρ explains why one hand would not do. θηρίον is ‘wild animal, beast’, here the stag, and μάλα … μέγα is ‘very great’.

sentences.t:
κὰδ’ δ’ ἔβαλον προπάροιθε νεός, ἀνέγειρα δ’ ἑταίρους
μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι παρασταδὸν ἄνδρα ἕκαστον·
sentences.tr:
kad’ d’ ebalon proparoithe neos, anegeira d’ hetairous
meilichiois epeessi parastadon andra hekaston·
sentences.l:
And down I cast it in front of the ship, and roused my companions
with gentle words, standing-beside each man:
sentences.i: I cast it down in front of the ship and roused my companions with gentle words, standing beside each man:
sentences.n: The colon marks that a speech follows in the next part; the line itself has no quoted words. κὰδ δ’ ἔβαλον is tmesis for ‘cast down’, as at 9.482 of the Cyclops’s stone; the archive prints κὰδ’ δ’ with an apostrophe the sense does not need, and the text is kept as printed. προπάροιθε is ‘in front of’, with the genitive νεός. ἀνέγειρα is the aorist of ἀνεγείρω ‘rouse’. μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι is ‘with gentle words’, the stock phrase, and παρασταδόν ‘standing beside’, with ἄνδρα ἕκαστον ‘each man’.
